items.text: Agent-manager is HTTP-only (gorilla/mux). No gRPC dependency or service definitions exist. Adding gRPC for verification would require introducing the full gRPC stack (grpc-go, protoc service generation, etc.).

packages/cli-core has zero external dependencies (stdlib only). JWT libraries like golang-jwt/jwt would be the first external dep, propagating to every scenario that imports cli-core. HMAC-SHA256 verification uses only crypto/hmac + crypto/sha256 from stdlib.

The injection point is ready: RunExecutor.SandboxEnvVars() returns map[string]string merged into ExecuteRequest.Environment. A parallel IdentityEnvVars() method would slot in alongside it with no structural changes needed.
Downstream execute items already exist (agent-manager-identity-tokens, swarm-manager-identity-adoption) waiting on this research. The conclusions here directly feed their implementation plans.

items.topic: Token format: JWT vs custom HMAC-signed payload
items.context: JWT brings standard tooling, well-known structure, and ecosystem interop — but adds golang-jwt as a dependency to cli-core (breaking its zero-external-deps stance) and is slightly oversized for this use case. A custom HMAC-SHA256 signed payload (base64-encoded JSON + HMAC signature) uses only stdlib, keeps tokens compact, and is simpler to implement — but is non-standard and requires documenting the format ourselves. Both are ~300-500 bytes in env vars.

options.label: Custom HMAC-SHA256 signed payload (stdlib only)
options.rationale: Preserves cli-core's zero-external-deps property. Simpler implementation. Format: base64(json_claims) + '.' + base64(hmac_sha256). Downside: non-standard, must document format ourselves.

options.label: JWT with HMAC-SHA256 (HS256)
options.rationale: Industry standard, well-understood claims structure, ecosystem of debugging tools (jwt.io). Downside: adds golang-jwt dependency to cli-core or requires a separate verification package.

options.label: JWT but only in agent-manager; cli-core gets opaque token + REST verification
options.rationale: Agent-manager uses golang-jwt internally for signing. cli-core never parses the token — it just passes it to a verification endpoint. Preserves cli-core's zero-dep stance while using standard JWT format. Downside: every verification requires a network call.

items.context: Self-verifiable tokens let consumers check signatures locally without network calls (requires sharing a secret or public key). Server-side verification means consumers send the token to agent-manager which confirms validity and returns claims. Since HMAC is symmetric, sharing the secret with every scenario is a security concern. Asymmetric signing (RS256/Ed25519) enables local verification without sharing private keys but adds complexity.

options.label: Server-side verification (opaque to consumers)
options.rationale: Simplest and most secure — consumers never see the signing key. Verification is a single HTTP call to agent-manager. Downside: adds latency and requires agent-manager to be reachable.

options.label: Self-verifiable with shared HMAC secret
options.rationale: No network calls needed. But sharing the HMAC secret with every scenario means any scenario could forge tokens. Only viable if all scenarios are fully trusted.

options.label: Self-verifiable with asymmetric keys (Ed25519)
options.rationale: Agent-manager signs with private key, scenarios verify with public key. No secret sharing, no network calls. But adds asymmetric crypto complexity and key distribution.

items.context: Given that agent-manager is HTTP-only today, should the verification endpoint be REST (consistent with existing API) or should we introduce gRPC for this? CLI consumers currently interact with agent-manager via REST through packages/cli-core/apiclient.go.

options.label: REST endpoint (POST /api/v1/identity/verify)
options.rationale: Consistent with existing HTTP API. cli-core already has an HTTP client (apiclient.go). No new dependencies. Simple to implement and test.

options.label: gRPC endpoint
options.rationale: Strongly typed contract, efficient binary protocol. But requires introducing gRPC stack to both agent-manager and cli-core — significant new dependency for a single endpoint.

items.context: The spec suggests minimum claims of run_id, task_id, profile_key, scope_path, issued_at, expires_at. Extended claims could include spawning_scenario (which scenario spawned the agent), initiative (for swarm-manager provenance), and agent_capabilities. More claims = more useful but also more coupling between agent-manager and consuming scenarios.

options.label: Minimal core claims + extensible metadata field
options.rationale: Core: run_id, task_id, profile_key, scope_path, issued_at, expires_at. Plus a generic 'metadata' map for scenario-specific claims like initiative or spawning_scenario. Keeps the standard lean while allowing extension.

options.label: Fixed extended claims set
options.rationale: Include all known useful claims: run_id, task_id, profile_key, scope_path, spawning_scenario, initiative, issued_at, expires_at. Simple and predictable but requires standard updates to add new claims.

Findings cover: HTTP-only architecture, cli-core zero-dep constraint, sandbox.go consumer pattern, injection point readiness, current string-only attribution, and token size analysis.
